articles.title: The Taíno story does not end neatly with “extinction.”
articles.summary: Archaeology, living heritage and genetic research ask different questions. Treating them as one verdict obscures both colonial catastrophe and the limits of what we know about Jamaica.

articles.title: Tacky’s revolt was a war with more than one front.
articles.summary: Vincent Brown’s interpretation moves beyond one leader and one parish to examine African politics, Jamaican terrain and imperial conflict together.

articles.title: 1938 was made by workers. Women belong in the account.
articles.summary: Party leaders, wage records, oral testimony and Sistren’s theatre offer different views of the upheaval. Recovering women requires more than adding a heroine to the familiar political story.

articles.title: Obeah: the accusation has a history too.
articles.summary: Court categories and colonial ideas shaped what counted as Obeah. Diana Paton’s research asks us to investigate the label as well as the people placed beneath it.

articles.title: Black Jamaicans helped make Christianity their own.
articles.summary: George Liele, Moses Baker and Black congregations complicate a story in which Europeans supplied religion and Jamaicans merely received it.

articles.title: The Jamaican diaspora did not begin at Tilbury.
articles.summary: Panama and the wider Caribbean basin restore a migration history that a Windrush-only narrative compresses. Work records reveal both movement and unequal treatment.

articles.title: The postcard Jamaica was made, not simply found.
articles.summary: Krista Thompson’s work shows how photographs helped construct the tropical destination. Historical pictures must be read as authored evidence rather than transparent windows.
